data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A panel of trained non-experts following an explicit checklist will produce more reliable judgments than a single expert relying on intuition because the checklist transforms the task from high-dimensional pattern recognition (prone to cognitive bias) into a series of low-dimensional binary verifications (resistant to bias).","counterconditions":[{"case":"The task requires the integration of non-linear variables that cannot be decomposed into a checklist without losing essential context.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist is insufficiently granular to capture the critical failure modes of the task.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The panel suffers from 'groupthink' or social pressure that overrides the checklist's objective prompts.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'cognitive decomposition': the checklist forces the panel to decouple the objective outcome from the expert's 'gestalt' intuition. While the expert processes the problem as a single, opaque pattern (which can be skewed by availability heuristics or fatigue), the panel processes it as a sum of discrete, verifiable gates. Reliability is gained by replacing the expert's singular point of failure (a biased intuition) with a redundant, additive system of error-traps.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
